title: Ethos, pathos and logos

draft.title: Ethos, pathos and logos
card: Persuaders use three kinds of appeal. Each one tries to win the audience in a different way.
an appeal to credibility. The speaker shows they are trustworthy, expert or fair, such as a doctor mentioning twenty years of treating patients.
an appeal to emotion. The speaker tries to make the audience feel pity, fear, pride or hope, often with vivid stories or loaded words.
an appeal to logic. The speaker uses facts, statistics and clear reasoning. Strong speeches balance all three appeals.
draft.remember: Ethos builds trust, pathos stirs feeling, logos gives reasons.

a.q: A principal tells parents that the school's exam results have risen every year for five years. Which appeal is mainly used?
opts: Logos, as it offers a fact as evidence
Ethos, as it shows the principal is a trusted leader
Pathos, as it makes parents feel proud of the school
Pathos, as it makes parents worry about their children
a.why: The statement gives a fact about results that can be checked, which is logos. It might also build trust, but its main job here is to give evidence rather than to show the speaker's character.
a.clue: Look for evidence that could be checked.

b.q: A speaker at a Tasmanian rally describes a lonely, shivering stray dog left outside in winter, then urges people to donate to an animal shelter. Which appeal is mainly used?
opts: Pathos, as the story is meant to stir pity
Logos, as the story is a reason to donate
Ethos, as the speaker shows love for animals
Logos, as the story is evidence of a real problem
b.why: The description of the shivering dog is designed to make the audience feel pity, so it is pathos. A story can sound like evidence, but it does not give facts or reasoning, so it is not logos.
b.clue: Ask what the audience is meant to feel.

a.best: Logos, as it offers a fact as evidence

b.best: Pathos, as the story is meant to stir pity
